    💡 Key Takeaways
    • South Korea's central bank on Thursday hiked benchmark lending rates to their highest in two years, as inflation continues to run above target while a booming economy allows it room to tighten policy.
    • The central bank raised rates by 25 basis points to 3.25% for its final meeting of the year, in line with expectations from economists, data on the Bank of Korea's website highlighted.
    • It has been revealed that inflation is expected to remain above its 2% target level for a considerable time, the BOK added in its statement, saying this was due to the pass-through of elevated cost pressures and as demand-side pressures also gradually strengthen, driven by stronger economic growth.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    South Korea's central bank on Thursday hiked benchmark lending rates to their highest in two years, as inflation continues to run above target while a booming economy allows it room to tighten policy.

    The central bank raised rates by 25 basis points to 3.25% for its final meeting of the year, in line with expectations from economists, data on the Bank of Korea's website highlighted.

    It has been revealed that inflation is expected to remain above its 2% target level for a considerable time, the BOK added in its statement, saying this was due to the pass-through of elevated cost pressures and as demand-side pressures also gradually strengthen, driven by stronger economic growth. Inflation in the country stood at 2.8% in October.

    The BOK also upgraded its growth forecasts for 2026 to 3.9% for 2026 and 4.1% for 2027, up from the 3.3% and 2.9%, respectively, forecast in August.

    South Korea's third-quarter GDP grew by 3.4% year on year, beating expectations, allowing the central bank room to raise rates.

    "The projections of high growth rates for next year and beyond also reflect the significantly increasing weight of the IT sector as a growth engine for the Korean economy," BOK Governor Shin Hyun-song mentioned at a press conference following the decision.

    Operating profits in the semiconductor sector could reach 700 trillion won, Shin told reporters, according to local news agency Yonhap.

    Shin also signaled that more rate hikes, although he did not give a fixed timeline.

    Recent findings suggest that "While the domestic economy is expected to continue its robust growth, inflation is forecast to remain above the target level for a considerable time ... The Board, therefore, sees it warranted to continue its policy response until there is confidence that inflation will converge stably to the target level.".

    Gareth Leather, senior Asia Economist at Capital Economics said there is reason to believe that the BOK's tightening cycle was drawing to a close.

    The BOK has raised rates by 75 basis points in five months, as higher energy prices from the Iran war and the AI boom has pushed up inflation in the country.

    Leather said that the country's strong growth, as well as a strengthening won could ease concerns over inflation.

    While rapidly rising property prices could strengthen the case for a prolonged tightening cycle, Leather mentioned that the BOK was "more likely to favour macroprudential measures over further rate hikes to address its financial stability concerns.".

    After the decision, the country's benchmark Kospi rose 1.88%.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.
    • Recent findings suggest that here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept.
    • Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

    Recent findings suggest that here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

    Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

    Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

    Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly vital sources of transaction revenue, while the tech giant has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

    Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

    Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

    Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

    Recent findings suggest that net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

    —With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney.

    Beware higher correlation but nab high U.S. credit yields, fund managers say

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The artificial intelligence boom could lead to a recession, whether through a collapse in AI investment or widespread job losses as the technology advances, a hedge fund manager mentioned.
    • "I do worry that if we don't have an AI-led recession in a few years, we're going to have an unemployment-led recession," Sheru Chowdhry, founder and chief investment officer at DSC Meridian Capital, said during a panel discussion moderated by CNBC's Joanna Ossinger at the iConnections Global Alts Asia conference in Singapore last week.
    • Chowdhry's warning highlights a risk that extends beyond a potential bursting of the AI bubble.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The artificial intelligence boom could lead to a recession, whether through a collapse in AI investment or widespread job losses as the technology advances, a hedge fund manager mentioned.

    "I do worry that if we don't have an AI-led recession in a few years, we're going to have an unemployment-led recession," Sheru Chowdhry, founder and chief investment officer at DSC Meridian Capital, said during a panel discussion moderated by CNBC's Joanna Ossinger at the iConnections Global Alts Asia conference in Singapore last week.

    Chowdhry's warning highlights a risk that extends beyond a potential bursting of the AI bubble. Rapid advances in the technology could lead to widespread job losses, with implications for the housing market and consumer spending, he said.

    "If this continues to go at the pace it is, I think in a few years a lot of us will probably not have jobs," Chowdhry stated, adding that investors would have to rethink their approach to sectors such as housing and discretionary spending.

    Even so, the fund manager remains bullish on computing power and sees opportunities in data centers, despite concerns about AI valuations.

    The current AI investment cycle reminds Chowdhry of the dot-com bubble and the telecommunications infrastructure buildout of the early 2000s.

    "This cycle reminds me of the dot-com bubble and the telecom build we had going on in the early 2000s," he said. "Every cycle is different, but it kind of rhymes in some ways.".

    Chowdhry also questioned whether semiconductor companies could sustain their profit margins in the coming years.

    However, he sees opportunities in data centers, pointing to access to power and grid connections as major bottlenecks in the AI buildout.

    "If you can identify data centers, I feel like that's going to be the picks and shovels of this cycle," he said.

    In particular, data centers that can secure permits and access to power within the next two years present a significant investment opportunity, he added.

    Beyond AI infrastructure, Chowdhry also pointed to attractive yields in U.S. credit markets.

    It has been revealed that he cited yields of around 8.5% on U.S. high-yield bonds and 9.5% on leveraged loans, describing the current market environment as an opportunity to "get paid to wait.".

    Investment portfolios may be more vulnerable to market volatility than they appear, according to Dan Gelernter, director of AI at R.G. Niederhoffer Capital Management, who spoke on the same panel.

    Average monthly correlations across investable assets rose from around 5% between the 1960s and 1990s to roughly 11% to 12% by 2020, according to research cited by Gelernter.

    His own analysis suggests that the figure has climbed further to around 15% to 16% in 2026.

    "Most portfolios are more highly levered, less liquid, more highly correlated than they appear to be, and that problem will get worse the more markets move," Gelernter said.

    Within the AI trade, Joo Kian Ong, a partner at AP3X Capital, noted Samsung Electronics would be a good long position, with SK Hynix or Micron on the other side as potential shorts.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.
    • Welcome to the latest edition of "Inside India" — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.
    • Despite 2026 being a challenging year with high global energy prices and supply chain disruptions, the Indian economy has fared surprisingly well.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.

    Welcome to the latest edition of "Inside India" — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.

    Despite 2026 being a challenging year with high global energy prices and supply chain disruptions, the Indian economy has fared surprisingly well. The auto industry, a key pillar of manufacturing and employment, has breached several records this year and is poised to report its best-ever sales.

    This week, I spoke to experts to decode what this stellar performance means for one of the world's most promising consumer markets.

    According to recent reports, any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team.

    Recent findings suggest that india's economy expanded at 7.8% in the June quarter, beating expectations, even as growth in several major economies cooled. Foreign portfolio investors who had been exiting Indian markets in droves for most of the year have also started returning in historic numbers.

    And now, the world's third-largest auto market is set to for a record this year as better road connectivity, tax cuts, and easier financing options have fueled bumper sales over the last several months. That comes at a time when major auto markets across the world, from China to the U.S. have been seeing a slump in sales.

    "10 years ago, despite having the money, people did not buy cars, but now even if they don't have the money, they take financing and buy," Amar Sheth, vice president of the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations, told CNBC, pointing to the shift in consumer mindset.

    They are becoming "more optimistic" about the future and, rather than waiting, consumers are willing to take a loan and purchase something useful to them now, he adds.

    The industry body that Sheth represents stated on Monday that automakers in India were poised to sell more than 30 million vehicles in the financial year ending March 2027, dubbing the sector as a "reflection of the wider India growth story.".

    From April to October, total vehicle retail sales in India reached 18.7 million units, up 10% from a year earlier, with car, tractor and commercial vehicle sales growing more than 15%, as per FADA data.

    The optimism of the industry body is also shared by major automakers; several of whom have declared capacity expansion looks this year to meet the growing consumer demand.

    Recent findings suggest that japanese automakers Maruti Suzuki and Toyota plan to raise capacity by 1.2 million units and 200,000 units, while Korea's Hyundai Motors will add capacity for 150,000 units, as per data shared by automotive industry intelligence provider Mobility Global. Leading Indian companies Tata Motors, Mahindra & Mahindra and JSW have also declared capacity addition plans, the data indicated.

    India is the only big auto market in the world that is growing while most others such as France, Germany, and Korea are "either declining or are flat," Puneet Gupta, director India and ASEAN at Mobility Global, told CNBC, explaining the reason behind car companies investing in the country.

    Gupta remarked that the Chinese automotive market hit an inflection point in 2007, when the GDP per capita crossed $2,500, and now India is "at a similar point." He added that government support for the auto industry would be crucial in replicating the boom seen in the Chinese auto industry.

    The catalyst for India's auto sector boom traces back to last September, when the government announced a wide range of tax cuts to spur domestic consumption.

    The auto industry contributes 7.1% to the country's gross domestic product, 49% to manufacturing GDP, 15% to goods and services tax collection, and supports 30 million jobs, as per government data.

    While the tailwinds from the tax cuts have faded, experts now believe that replacement demand and the growing reach of financing options to smaller cities will unlock the next phase of growth.

    Consumption has been strong this year as the government has partly shielded people from rising energy costs while corporates, with their strong balance sheets, have been slow to pass on price hikes, Gaura Sengupta, chief economist at India's IDFC First Bank, noted.

    So far this year, wage growth has been good, the labor market has held up equity markets haven't corrected sharply, keeping the wealth effect intact, she said, underscoring the reasons driving consumption along with easy access to credit.

    Despite the economy facing external shocks, producers are also "feeling confident to add capacity" as they have seen domestic demand sustain, Sengupta added.

    However, experts mentioned that the central bank's recent tightening of monetary policy and price hikes by automakers could slightly take the edge off the auto sales boom in the last few months of the financial year.

    While urban demand is unlikely to get affected, rural sales growth could moderate, they added.

    "Overall retail should close FY27 in high single digits," Diwakar Murugan, senior automotive analyst at Omdia, told CNBC, adding that this year's record sales are not a one-time spike but a "structural reset.".

    China has changed tactics but is still thwarting India's rise, a U.S. panel saysChina is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.

    U.K.-India trade deal faces a stiff test over Scotch whisky import taxesWithin months of taking effect, the India-U.K. trade deal is facing an early test, as Fresh Delhi resists extending preferential tariffs to bulk Scotch whisky imports.

    In a recent development, investors give a thumbs down to Tata Steel-APL Apollo $1.67 billion deal, plunging sharesTata Steel, one of the world's leading steel producers, on Monday said it will buy a 26.4% stake in India's largest structural steel pipe and tube maker, APL Apollo, for 155.1 billion rupees ($1.67 billion). However, investors reacted negatively to the deal.

    In a recent development, nov. 27: Mahanadi Coalfields IPO listing.
